claim: Meniscus degeneration is a major origin of knee osteoarthritis.
source: Meniscus degeneration is a major origin of knee osteoarthritis and a common threat to athletic ability, but its cellular mechanism remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information without specific data or citation in this sentence.

claim: A cell atlas of 12 healthy or degenerated human meniscus samples from 8 patients was built using scRNA-seq.
source: We built a cell atlas of 12 healthy or degenerated human meniscus samples from the inner and outer meniscal zones of 8 patients using scRNA-seq to investigate meniscal microenvironment homeostasis and its changes in the degeneration process and verified findings with immunofluorescent imaging.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection performed in the study.

claim: New chondrocyte subtypes associated with degeneration were identified.
source: We identified and localized cell types in inner and outer meniscus and found new chondrocyte subtypes associated with degeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the scRNA-seq analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: There are possible loop-like interactions among extracellular matrix disassembly, angiogenesis, and inflammation in driving meniscal degeneration.
source: The observations suggested understandings on how cellular compositions, functions, and interactions participated in degeneration, and on the possible loop-like interactions among extracellular matrix disassembly, angiogenesis, and inflammation in driving the degeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the data analysis and observations in the study.

claim: Nearly half of patients with meniscal degeneration will eventually develop OA over time.
source: It has been found through clinical observations that nearly half of patients with meniscal degeneration will eventually develop OA over time (Lohmander et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lohmander et al., 2007.

claim: Inflammatory responses and biomineralization affect the meniscus cellular microenvironment and contribute to disease occurrence.
source: Studies have shown that inflammatory responses and biomineralization affect the meniscus cellular microenvironment and contribute to disease occurrence (Sun et al., 2010; Goldring and Goldring, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2010 and Goldring and Goldring, 2016.

claim: The meniscus can be anatomically divided into the inner region (the white–white zone) and the outer region (the red–red zone).
source: The meniscus can be anatomically divided into the inner region (the white–white zone) and the outer region (the red–red zone).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about meniscus structure.

claim: There are blood vessels and nerves in the outer area of the meniscus, while few blood vessels and nerves are observed in the inner part.
source: There are blood vessels and nerves in the outer area, while few blood vessels and nerves are observed in the inner part.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about meniscus vascularization.

claim: The outer meniscus is dominated by type I collagen, while the inner meniscus is dominated by type II collagen.
source: The outer meniscus is dominated by type I collagen, while the inner meniscus is dominated by type II collagen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ECM composition of meniscus zones.

claim: The inner part of the meniscus has a relatively higher percentage of PGs compared with the outer.
source: The inner part of the meniscus has a relatively higher percentage of PGs compared with the outer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ECM composition of meniscus zones.

claim: The degeneration in the outer meniscus is more likely to heal, while the degeneration in the inner part tends to be irreversible.
source: Different anatomical regions have varied recovery capabilities: the degeneration in the outer meniscus is more likely to heal, while the degeneration in the inner part tends to be irreversible (Makris et al., 2011; Danzig et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makris et al., 2011 and Danzig et al., 1983.

claim: Ghadially et al., 1983 stated that chondrocytes, a few fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and intermediate state cells between chondrocytes and fibroblast existed in menisci.
source: They studied injured and uninjured human menisci with the electron microscope and stated that chondrocytes, a few fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, and intermediate state cells between chondrocytes and fibroblast existed in menisci.
evidence: This references historical work by Ghadially et al., 1983 on meniscal cell types.

claim: Cells in the superficial zone of the meniscus were fusiform, while cells laid deeper were polygonal.
source: Scotti et al. also discussed that the cells in the superficial zone were fusiform, while cells laid deeper were polygonal (Scotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This references work by Scotti et al., 2013 on meniscal cell morphology.

claim: Sun et al., 2020 reported cartilage progenitor cells (CPC), regulatory chondrocytes (RegC), prehypertrophic chondrocytes (PreHTC), hypertrophic chondrocytes (HTC), fibrochondrocytes (FC), fibrochondrocytes progenitors (FCP), proliferating fibrochondrocytes (ProFC), degenerated progenitor (DegP), endothelial cells, and other immune cells in the meniscus.
source: They reported cartilage progenitor cells (CPC), regulatory chondrocytes (RegC), prehypertrophic chondrocytes (PreHTC), hypertrophic chondrocytes (HTC), fibrochondrocytes (FC), fibrochondrocytes progenitors (FCP), proliferating fibrochondrocytes (ProFC), degenerated progenitor (DegP), endothelial cells, and other immune cells in the meniscus, and showed links between meniscus progenitors and the progression of meniscal degeneration (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This references findings from Sun et al., 2020 on meniscal cell types.

claim: The study created a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of 45,744 cells from 12 healthy/degenerated meniscus samples of 8 patients.
source: We created a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of 45,744 cells from 12 healthy/degenerated meniscus samples of 8 patients and provided an online cell browser at http://meni.singlecell.info:3000/ to support flexible explorations of the data.
evidence: This describes the dataset generated in the study.

claim: Five chondrocyte subtypes and two pericyte-like cell subtypes were identified.
source: We built a hierarchical cell type classification framework and identified five chondrocyte subtypes and two pericyte-like cell subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cell type classification analysis.

claim: Damage-induced inflammatory responses were observed in degenerated samples.
source: We profiled various immune cell types and observed damage-induced inflammatory responses in degenerated samples.
evidence: This is an observation from the immune cell profiling analysis.

claim: Four degenerative meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with severe OA who underwent total knee arthroplasty.
source: Four degenerative meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with severe OA who underwent total knee arthroplasty, and four normal meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with bone tumors or severe trauma who underwent amputation.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: Four normal meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with bone tumors or severe trauma who underwent amputation.
source: Four degenerative meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with severe OA who underwent total knee arthroplasty, and four normal meniscus specimens were obtained from patients with bone tumors or severe trauma who underwent amputation.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: The meniscus tissues were removed from the patient's knee joints and divided into the inner (white–white zone) and outer (red–red zone) areas.
source: The meniscus tissues were removed from the patient's knee joints and divided into the inner (white–white zone) and outer (red–red zone) areas.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation methodology.

claim: 0.25% Trypsin was used to digest the meniscus pieces for 0.5 hr under 37℃.
source: We used 0.25% Trypsin (Gibco 25200072) to digest the pieces for 0.5 hr under 37℃.
evidence: This describes the tissue dissociation protocol.

claim: 2 mg/ml collagenase IV was used to dissociate the meniscus pieces for 4–6 hr under 37℃.
source: Next, we used 2 mg/ml collagenase IV to dissociate the pieces for 4–6 hr under 37℃ and finally obtained dissociated cells.
evidence: This describes the tissue dissociation protocol.

claim: The dissociated cells were resuspended at a concentration of 250–1200 cells/μl with viability between 67–87% for microfluidics.
source: The dissociated cells were resuspended at a concentration of 250–1200 cells/μl and with viability between 67–87% for microfluidics (Chromium Single-Cell Controller, 10× Genomics).
evidence: This describes the cell preparation for single-cell sequencing.

claim: Cells were loaded into the chip and run using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kit v2 (10× Genomics).
source: According to the manufacturer's instructions, cells were loaded into the chip and run using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent Kit v2 (10× Genomics).
evidence: This describes the single-cell sequencing platform used.

claim: Sequencing-ready single-cell transcriptome libraries were mapped to the human reference genome GRCh38-3.0.0 and quantified by CellRanger 3.1.0.
source: Sequencing-ready single-cell transcriptome libraries were mapped to the human reference genome GRCh38-3.0.0 and quantified by CellRanger 3.1.0.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics pipeline for data processing.

claim: Ambient RNA expression was adjusted with SoupX v1.2.1.
source: We adjusted the ambient RNA expression with SoupX (Young and Behjati, 2020) v1.2.1 and generated read counts free of background noises for all downstream analyses.
evidence: This describes a quality control step in the data analysis pipeline.

claim: Scanpy and Seurat were used to conduct basic filtering of outlier cells.
source: We used scanpy (Wolf et al., 2018) and Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019; Butler et al., 2018) to conduct the basic filtering out outliers cells with high n_genes metrics (the number of observed genes per cell), high n_counts metrics (the number of UMI per cell), and high percent_mito metrics (the mitochondrial gene fraction).
evidence: This describes quality control methods using established software tools.

claim: Draft cell type identities were assigned to cells using SingleR.
source: Next, we assigned draft cell type identities to the cells using SingleR (Aran et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a cell type annotation method used in the analysis.

claim: Doublet scores were calculated using DoubletFinder and cells with high doublet scores were removed.
source: We calculated doublet scores using DoubletFinder (McGinnis et al., 2019) removed the cells with high doublet scores and outlier clusters with high doublet scores.
evidence: This describes a quality control step to remove doublets.

claim: Dissociation scores were calculated using methods described in van den Brink et al., 2017.
source: We calculated dissociation scores using methods described in van den Brink et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes a quality control method to assess dissociation-induced gene expression.

claim: Harmony was used to perform integrative clustering across different samples to eliminate genetic background variations and technical noises.
source: To eliminate the genetic background variations and technical noises of the single-cell RNA-seq data, we used Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) to perform integrative clustering across different samples.
evidence: This describes the batch correction method used in the analysis.

claim: Major clusters corresponded to chondral cells, ACTA2+ cells, endothelial cells, and immune cells were identified across samples.
source: Major clusters corresponded to chondral cells, ACTA2+ cells, endothelial cells, and immune cells were identified across samples and validated with cluster correlation analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the clustering analysis, supported by figures.

claim: MetaCell was used to partition original cell data points into homogenous meta-cells.
source: To alleviate the scRNA-seq data noise and promote data consistency across samples (Hua and Zhang, 2019), we partitioned original cell data points into homogenous meta-cells with MetaCell (Baran et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a data processing method used in the analysis.

claim: HGC was used to build hierarchical relationships based on the meta-cells.
source: We then used HGC (Zou et al., 2021) to build hierarchical relationships based on the meta-cells.
evidence: This describes a hierarchical clustering method used in the analysis.

claim: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified by the 'FindMarkers' function and the 'FindAllMarkers' function provided by the Seurat package.
source: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified by the 'FindMarkers' function and the 'FindAllMarkers' function provided by the Seurat package.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying differentially expressed genes.

claim: Enrichment analyses were performed with top fold-change DEGs and a BH-adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05, using R package clusterProfiler.
source: Enrichment analyses were performed with top fold-change DEGs and a BH-adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05, using R package clusterProfiler (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the method for gene set enrichment analysis.

claim: Gene set activity scores were assigned to individual cells using gene set variation analysis (GSVA).
source: We assigned gene set activity scores to individual cells using gene set variation analysis (GSVA) (Hänzelmann et al., 2013), with gene sets obtained from MSigDB (Subramanian et al., 2005; Liberzon et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating gene set activity scores.

claim: pySCENIC was used to infer gene regulatory networks (GRN) from single-cell expressional profiles.
source: We used the python package pySCENIC (Van de Sande et al., 2020; Aibar et al., 2017) to infer gene regulatory networks (GRN) from single-cell expressional profiles.
evidence: This describes the method for gene regulatory network inference.

claim: Meniscal specimens in the normal group are smooth and complete with a clear structure.
source: Figure 1A illustrates the morphological patterns of the samples: Meniscal specimens in the normal group are smooth and complete with a clear structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the specimen photographs in Figure 1A.

claim: Specimens from the degenerated group are swollen, irregular in shape, damaged in structure, and vascularized.
source: Specimens from the degenerated group are swollen, irregular in shape, damaged in structure, and vascularized.
evidence: This is an observation from the specimen photographs in Figure 1A.

claim: 45,744 cells were recovered from 12 samples of 8 patients after quality control.
source: After comprehensive quality control steps removing low-quality cells and inferred doublets (Methods), we recovered 45,744 cells from 12 samples of 8 patients (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This reports the final cell count after quality control.

claim: Five major cell types were observed in the inner menisci: chondrocytes, lymphocytes, myeloid cells, endothelial cells, and a group of ACTA2+ cells.
source: We observed five major cell types in the inner menisci: chondrocytes, lymphocytes, myeloid cells, endothelial cells, and a group of ACTA2+ cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cell type identification analysis.

claim: The outer menisci had the five cell types observed in inner menisci plus a group of Schwann cells.
source: We also observed the five types in the outer menisci, plus a group of Schwann cells, indicating there are nerve tissues in the outer menisci.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cell type identification analysis.

claim: The outer menisci had higher cell type diversities compared to inner menisci.
source: The percentages of cells in Figure 1E, H showed that, in general, the outer menisci had higher cell type diversities.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell type composition analysis shown in figures.

claim: In the more diverse outer menisci, the degenerated group had higher immune cell ratios and lower ACTA2+ cell ratios.
source: In the more diverse outer menisci, the degenerated group (A1, B2, and D2) had higher immune cell ratios and lower ACTA2+ cell ratios.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell type composition analysis.

claim: Cell clusters were identified as chondrocytes if they expressed a high level of cartilage-related genes such as DCN, PRG4, COL1A2, COL3A1, ACAN, COMP, FN1, CHI3L1, and CHI3L2.
source: We identified cell clusters as chondrocytes if they expressed a high level of cartilage-related genes such as DCN, PRG4, COL1A2, COL3A1, ACAN, COMP, FN1, CHI3L1, and CHI3L2.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying chondrocytes based on marker gene expression.

claim: Cell clusters with high expression levels of PLVAP and PECAM1 were identified as endothelial cells.
source: We identified cell clusters with high expression levels of PLVAP, PECAM1 as endothelial cells.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying endothelial cells based on marker gene expression.

claim: Immune cells were identified using high PTPRC, myeloid markers CD68, C1QA, HLA-DQA1, and T cell markers CD3D, CD3E.
source: Immune cells were identified using high PTPRC, myeloid markers CD68, C1QA, HLA-DQA1, and T cell markers CD3D, CD3E.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying immune cells based on marker gene expression.

claim: A group of cells separated from other cells in both inner and outer areas of the meniscus has high expression levels of ACTA2 and was tentatively named 'pericyte-like cells' or PCL.
source: In addition, there are a group of cells separated from other cells in both inner and outer areas of the meniscus, which has high expression levels of ACTA2. Besides high expressions of ACTA2, this group of cells also expressed some chondrocyte-associated gene markers, such as COL1A2, COL3A1, DCN, and FN1. We tentatively named this ACTA2+ group 'pericyte-like cells' or PCL (Figure 1I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B) and reanalyzed them together with the chondrocytes in Figure 2 and associated texts.
evidence: This describes the identification and naming of a novel cell population based on marker expression.

claim: Five chondral clusters named chondrocyte-1 to chondrocyte-5 (Ch.1–Ch.5) and two pericyte-like cell clusters (PCL.1 and PCL.2) were identified.
source: We finally identified five chondral clusters named chondrocyte-1 to chondrocyte-5 (Ch.1–Ch.5 in Figure 2A) and two pericyte-like cell clusters (PCL.1 and PCL.2 in Figure 2A) named ACTA2+ cells in Figure 1D, G.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the hierarchical cell type classification.

claim: Common fibroblast markers like DCN and LUM are highly expressed in the chondral class.
source: Common fibroblast markers like DCN and LUM are highly expressed in the chondral class.
evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis.

claim: Smooth muscle cell and pericyte markers like ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYL9 are highly expressed in the PCL class.
source: Smooth muscle cell and pericyte markers like ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYL9 are highly expressed in the PCL class.
evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis.

claim: The PCL cells present strong muscle contractile gene expression signatures including ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN.
source: The PCL cells present strong muscle contractile gene expression signatures (Figure 2F), including ACTA2, MYL9, TAGLN, etc.
evidence: This is an observation from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ACTA2 encodes a smooth muscle actin involved in vascular contractility.
source: ACTA2, which encodes a smooth muscle actin involved in vascular contractility, as well as TAGLN (transgelin) and MYH/MYL (myosin heavy/light chains) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of ACTA2.

claim: ACTA2, TAGLN, and MYH/MYL genes have been used for identifying pericytes or smooth muscle cells across multiple human organs.
source: These genes have been used for identifying pericytes or smooth muscle cells across multiple human organs, including intervertebral disc (Gan et al., 2021), intestinal tract (Elmentaite et al., 2021), heart (Litvinukova et al., 2020), brain (Smyth et al., 2018), etc.
evidence: This references multiple studies that have used these markers for cell identification.

claim: Gene set enrichment analyses of PCL signature genes suggested the PCL population has a discrepant molecular identity from the chondrocyte lineage.
source: The gene set enrichment analyses of these signature genes suggested the PCL population has a discrepant molecular identity from the chondrocyte lineage because GO terms such as 'muscle contraction', 'muscle organ development', and 'smooth muscle cell proliferation' were enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is an inference from the gene set enrichment analysis results.

claim: Sun et al., 2020 named a similar ACTA2+ MYLK+ MCAM+ MYL9+ cluster as the FCP and claimed FCP could differentiate into degenerated meniscus progenitors (DegP) in degenerated menisci.
source: In the work of Sun et al., 2020, they named a similar ACTA2+ MYLK+ MCAM+ MYL9+cluster as the FCP and claimed FCP could differentiate into degenerated meniscus progenitors (DegP) in degenerated menisci, or into adipogenic/osteogenic lineages when cultured ex vivo.
evidence: This references findings from Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The PCL population in the current study showed weak differentiation potential into DegP because this group of cells did not show concentrated expressions of DegP markers GREM1, CDCP1, and DNER.
source: We did not name the population we found as FCP for three reasons: Firstly, enrichment analyses showed its similarity to pericytes/smooth muscle cells. Secondly, our PCL population showed weak differentiation potential into DegP because this group of cells in our data did not show concentrated expressions of DegP markers GREM1, CDCP1, and DNER.
evidence: This is an observation from the marker gene expression analysis comparing to Sun et al., 2020.

claim: The PCL cells are more abundant in the vascularized outer meniscus region than in the avascular inner part.
source: The PCL cells are more abundant in the vascularized outer meniscus region than in the avascular inner part (Figure 1E, H).
evidence: This is an observation from the cell composition analysis shown in figures.

claim: Immunofluorescence imaging found that PCL cells lay around the vascular endothelial cells and formed a tube shape outside the blood vessels.
source: Our immunofluorescence imaging found that this population of cells lay around the vascular endothelial cells and formed a tube shape outside the blood vessels (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence imaging experiments.

claim: Gan et al., 2021 named a group of ACTA2+ MCAM+ TAGLN+ cells in the human intervertebral disc as pericytes.
source: Gan et al., 2021 named a group of ACTA2+ MCAM+ TAGLN+ in the human intervertebral disc as pericytes, which can be a reference for defining meniscal cell clusters.
evidence: This references findings from Gan et al., 2021 on intervertebral disc cell types.

claim: It is difficult to fully distinguish pericyte from smooth muscle cells purely based on the transcriptomes because the two cell types share numerous markers.
source: We admit that it is difficult to fully distinguish pericyte from smooth muscle cells purely based on the transcriptomes because the two cell types share numerous markers, and their markers appear to be dynamic and affected by the tissue types and pathogenic states (van Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: Pericytes attach to the surface of vascular endothelial cells and maintain vasculature stability via the endothelium–pericyte crosstalk.
source: It is known that pericytes attach to the surface of vascular endothelial cells and maintain vasculature stability via the endothelium–pericyte crosstalk (Eilken et al., 2017; Sugihara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte function, supported by citations.

claim: Pericytes have pro-angiogenesis capabilities.
source: Previous studies have shown that pericytes have pro-angiogenesis capabilities (Eilken et al., 2017; Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte function, supported by citations.

claim: Both PCL.1 and PCL.2 expressed ECM components Collagen IVα1 (COL4A1), Collagen IVα2 (COL4A2), and Collagen XVIII (COL18A1), the non-collagenous fragments of which were known to have anti-angiogenesis functions.
source: For example, in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, we showed that both PCL.1 and PCL.2 expressed ECM components Collagen IVα1 (COL4A1), Collagen IVα2 (COL4A2), and Collagen XVIII (COL18A1), the non-collagenous fragments of which (i.e., arresten, canstatin, and endostatin, respectively) were known to have anti-angiogenesis functions (de Castro Brás and Frangogiannis, 2020; Marneros and Olsen, 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Two subtle subclusters were identified within the PCL class: PCL.1 expresses a higher level of FABP4, RGS5, and PCL.2 has relatively higher expressions of MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN.
source: We identified two subtle subclusters within the PCL class. One subcluster PCL.1 expresses a higher level of FABP4, RGS5, and the other PCL.2 subcluster has relatively higher expressions of MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN.
evidence: This is a finding from the subclustering analysis of PCL cells.

claim: Kumar et al., 2017 analyzed FABP4, RGS5, MYH11, MYH9, CNN1, and TAGLN genes' functions in the specification and diversification of pericyte/smooth muscle cells from mesenchymoangioblasts.
source: Kumar et al., 2017 analyzed these genes' functions in the specification and diversification of pericyte/smooth muscle cells from mesenchymoangioblasts.
evidence: This references findings from Kumar et al., 2017 on pericyte/smooth muscle cell differentiation.

claim: PCL.1 had more active responses to the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and TNF-α.
source: The GSVA suggested that PCL.1 had more active responses to the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1 and TNF-α (Figure 2G) and expressed higher levels of chemokines genes CCL2, CCL19, CCL21, CXCL12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), and COL4A1/2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in figures.

claim: PCL.2 had higher myofibril gene set activation scores, indicating this population could have higher muscle contractility and may regulate the blood flow in the microvasculature.
source: The GSVA scores suggested that PCL.2 had higher myofibril gene set activation scores, indicating this population could have higher muscle contractility and may regulate the blood flow in the microvasculature (van Dijk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis, with functional interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: The largest chondrocyte branch is the chondrocyte-1 (Ch.1) population that highly expresses CHAD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, ECRG (C2orf40), and APOD.
source: The largest branch is the chondrocyte-1 (Ch.1) population that highly expresses CHAD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, ECRG (C2orf40), and APOD.
evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claim: Some Ch.1 marker genes (e.g., CHI3L1/2) have been described as the markers of RegC.
source: Some of these genes (e.g., CHI3L1/2) have been described as the markers of RegC (Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This references findings from Ji et al., 2019 on regulatory chondrocyte markers.

claim: Ch.1 cluster's percentage decreased in the degeneration group.
source: This cluster's percentage decreased in the degeneration group.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell composition analysis.

claim: Gene set activation analysis indicated that Ch.1 population had anti-angiogenesis effects.
source: The gene set activation analysis indicated that this population of cells had anti-angiogenesis effects (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ch.1 highly expressed ECM regulators TIMP1 and TIMP4, which were inhibitors of ECM destruction proteins.
source: ECM-related gene expressions indicated Ch.1 highly expressed ECM regulators TIMP1 and TIMP4, which were inhibitors of ECM destruction proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from ECM-related gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation based on known protein functions.

claim: The CHAD+ Ch.1 population is a cluster of chondrocytes that maintain homeostasis in the meniscal tissue.
source: Hence, we inferred that the CHAD+ Ch.1 population is a cluster of chondrocytes that maintain homeostasis in the meniscal tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression and functional analysis.

claim: Ch.3 cells express high levels of PRG4, HTRA1, FN1, CD55, TIMP3, CDON, AMTN.
source: We named another part of this branch that expresses high levels of PRG4, HTRA1, FN1, CD55, TIMP3, CDON, AMTN as Ch.3 (PRG4).
evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claim: Ch.3 cells had lubrication function because the protein proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) has a lubrification function on the articular cartilage surface.
source: We inferred that Ch.3 cells had lubrication function because the protein proteoglycan 4 (PRG4) has a lubrification function on the articular cartilage surface, and these cells were located near the surface of the meniscus.
evidence: This is an inference based on PRG4 function and cell localization.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that Ch.3 marker CDON expresses along the surface region of the meniscus.
source: Our immunofluorescence staining further confirmed that its marker CDON expresses along the surface region of the meniscus (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence imaging experiments.

claim: Ch.3 population highly expresses TIMP1/2/3 and may inhibit the matrix decomposition by opposing the MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family enzymes.
source: This population highly expresses TIMP1/2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and may inhibit the matrix decomposition by opposing the MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on TIMP expression and known TIMP function.

claim: Ch.2 population highly expresses OA marker genes and chondrocyte hypertrophy genes such as type I, III, and VI collagen genes (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1/2/3), POSTN, MMP2, SPARC, and MXRA5.
source: The Ch.2 population highly expresses OA marker genes (Fisch et al., 2018) and chondrocyte hypertrophy genes (Ji et al., 2019) such as type I, III, and VI collagen genes (COL1A1/2, COL3A1, COL6A1/2/3), POSTN, MMP2, SPARC, and MXRA5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation supported by citations.

claim: FNDC1 and MXRA5 have been recently reported as signatures of chondrocyte-mediated valve calcification in aortic stenosis.
source: Among these upregulated genes, FNDC1 and MXRA5 have been recently reported as signatures of chondrocyte-mediated valve calcification in aortic stenosis (Bouchareb et al., 2021).
evidence: This references findings from Bouchareb et al., 2021.

claim: MXRA5 (matrix remodeling-associated protein 5) is a TGF-β1 regulated gene.
source: It is also known that MXRA5 (matrix remodeling-associated protein 5) is a TGF-β1 regulated gene (Poveda et al., 2017), which is consistent with the high GSVA scores of 'Response to TGFβ' in Ch.2 shown in Figure 2G.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation, consistent with GSVA results.

claim: Ch.2 population expresses MMP, ADAM, and ADAMTS family genes, such as MMP11/13/14, ADAM9/12, and ADAMTS2, which can target collagen, aggrecans or other ECM components.
source: Besides MMP2, this population also expresses other MMP, ADAM, and ADAMTS family genes, such as MMP11/13/14, ADAM9/12, and ADAMTS2, which can target collagen, aggrecans or other ECM components (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from gene expression analysis, with functional interpretation based on known protein functions.

claim: Ch.2 (FNDC1) is a chondrocyte population associated with aberrant ECM degradation and remodeling, and this population may contribute to the progress of human meniscal degeneration.
source: The increased expression of these genes indicated that Ch.2 (FNDC1) is a chondrocyte population associated with aberrant ECM degradation and remodeling, and this population may contribute to the progress of human meniscal degeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression patterns and functional analysis.

claim: Ch.4 subcluster expresses high levels of CFD, CFH, C1R, C1S, CXCL12, and VCAN.
source: The other CFD+ subcluster in this branch expresses high levels of CFD, CFH, C1R, C1S, CXCL12, and VCAN. We name it Ch.4 (CFD).
evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claim: Ch.4 subcluster expresses genes associated with alternative complement activation pathways (C1R, C1S, C2, C3, C6, and C7) and may promote inflammation by recruiting macrophages and neutrophils.
source: This subcluster expresses genes associated with alternative complement activation pathways (C1R, C1S, C2, C3, C6, and C7) and may promote inflammation by recruiting macrophages and neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on complement gene expression and known complement functions.

claim: Ch.5 represents chondrocytes in proliferation states and highly expressed S- and G2M-phase cell-cycle genes such as STMN1, CDK1, CENPF, HMGB2, CDKN3, TOP2A.
source: Ch.5 represents chondrocytes in proliferation states. They highly expressed the S- and G2M-phase cell-cycle genes such as STMN1, CDK1, CENPF, HMGB2, CDKN3, TOP2A and were mostly found in the degenerated samples.
evidence: This is a finding from the chondrocyte subtype characterization.

claim: 98.63% Ch.5 cells were mapped to Ch.2 and the rest were mapped to Ch.3 using reference mapping analysis.
source: We re-assigned Ch.5 cell identities using cells in Ch.1–Ch.4 clusters as a reference with SingleR (Aran et al., 2019) and found 98.63% Ch.5 cells were mapped to Ch.2 and the rest were mapped to Ch.3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 7F).
evidence: This is a finding from the reference mapping analysis.

claim: The identity mapping suggested the proliferative Ch.5 could be the origin of the Ch.2 cells increased in the degenerated group.
source: This identity mapping suggested the proliferative Ch.5 could be the origin of the Ch.2 cells increased in the degenerated group.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reference mapping results.

claim: Genes upregulated in the degeneration group include COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN.
source: We identified genes upregulated in the degeneration group, such as COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN, and genes upregulated in the normal group, such as APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM (shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, an extended list of genes in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes upregulated in the normal group include APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM.
source: We identified genes upregulated in the degeneration group, such as COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL6A1, POSTN, SPARC, CILP, TGFBI, DPT, and ATMN, and genes upregulated in the normal group, such as APOD, CHI3L1, CHI3L2, CEBPD, C11orf96, C2orf40 (ECRG4), ACTA2, TAGLN, BCAM, and MCAM (shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, an extended list of genes in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The overall expression differences between normal and degenerated conditions are mainly contributed by the cell type compositional changes.
source: We believe the overall expression differences are mainly contributed by the cell type compositional changes because these genes are identified as markers of the chondrocyte subpopulations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between DEGs and cell type markers.

claim: Ch.2 and Ch.3 increased in degeneration while Ch.1 and PCL decreased in degeneration.
source: All these expression differences are consistent with our compositional observations that Ch.2 and Ch.3 increased in degeneration and Ch.1 and PCL decreased in degeneration (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell composition analysis.

claim: The overall expressional changes after degeneration could be explained by the increase of Ch.2 and Ch.3 as well as the decrease of PCL cells.
source: Considering all factors above, it appears that the overall expressional changes after degeneration could be explained by the increase of Ch.2 and Ch.3 as well as the decrease of PCL cells.
evidence: This is an inference integrating multiple observations.

claim: Ch.2 could have high ECM disassembly scores while Ch.3 could negatively regulate the disassembly regardless of the degeneration states.
source: We first analyzed the GSVA scores of ECM-related gene ontology terms in Figure 3C and found Ch.2 could have high ECM disassembly scores while Ch.3 could negatively regulate the disassembly regardless of the degeneration states.
evidence: This is an inference from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ch.2 and Ch.3 got high scores in leukocyte chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and chondrocyte hypertrophy-associated terms.
source: Ch.2 and Ch.3 also got high scores in leukocyte chemotaxis (Figure 3D), angiogenesis (Figure 3E), and chondrocyte hypertrophy-associated terms (Figure 3F); while in contrast, Ch.1 had relatively lower scores on these terms.
evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis shown in figures.

claim: Ch.5 got high scores on the cell-cycle-related terms.
source: Ch.5 got high scores on the cell-cycle-related terms (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PCL cells got higher pro-angiogenesis scores in degenerated samples than in normal samples.
source: PCL cells got higher pro-angiogenesis scores in degenerated samples than in normal samples.
evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis comparing conditions.

claim: The inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions after degeneration.
source: From the cell density plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A, B, we found that the inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions, while the outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions.
evidence: This is an observation from cell density analysis shown in figures.

claim: The outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions after degeneration.
source: From the cell density plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A, B, we found that the inner zone chondrocytes shift from the Ch.1 positions to the Ch.3 positions, while the outer zone chondrocytes shift to Ch.2 and Ch.4 positions.
evidence: This is an observation from cell density analysis shown in figures.

claim: The outer-degenerated groups consistently got significantly higher inflammation scores than the outer-normal group.
source: We also evaluated the GSVA scores of three inflammation gene sets on the chondrocytes and found the outer-degenerated groups consistently got significantly higher inflammation scores than the outer-normal group. In contrast, the inner zone cells did not have this trend (Figure 3—figure supplement 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from GSVA analysis of inflammation gene sets shown in figures.

claim: Outer menisci could contribute more to joint inflammation in OA.
source: From the computational analyses, we inferred that outer menisci could contribute more to joint inflammation in OA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inflammation score analysis.

claim: CDON+ chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue.
source: From the staining results, we can clearly find that CDON + chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue, and ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
source: From the staining results, we can clearly find that CDON + chondrocytes were mainly distributed on the surface of the meniscus tissue, and ACTA2+ pericytes were presented surrounding blood vessels.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: SERPINA1+, CYP1B1+, and MMP14+ chondrocytes were mixed and scattered inside the meniscus.
source: SERPINA1+, CYP1B1+, and MMP14+ chondrocytes were mixed and scattered inside the meniscus.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments.

claim: Immune cells were mainly distributed around the blood vessels in the meniscus.
source: Immune cells were mainly distributed around the blood vessels in the meniscus.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining experiments.

claim: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased in degenerative specimens.
source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claim: The number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased in degenerative specimens.
source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claim: The number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens.
source: Compared with the normal samples, the number of ACTA2+ chondrocytes was decreased, the number of MMP14+ chondrocytes was markedly increased, and the number of vascular endothelial cells was significantly increased in degenerative specimens (Figure 4A–H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence staining comparing normal and degenerated samples.

claim: Macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and cycling immune cells were identified in normal and degenerated meniscal samples.
source: For the leukocyte part, we identified macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, mast cells, dendritic cells, T cells, and cycling immune cells in normal and degenerated meniscal samples (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from immune cell profiling.

claim: Macrophage/monocyte makes up the largest portion of the total immune population.
source: Macrophage/monocyte makes up the largest portion of the total immune population.
evidence: This is an observation from immune cell composition analysis.

claim: The percentages of macrophage/monocyte, T cell, dendritic cell, and total immune cell increased in the degeneration group.
source: The percentages of macrophage/monocyte, T cell, dendritic cell, and total immune cell increased in the degeneration group, which was consistent with the vascularization and the damage-induced inflammation (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from immune cell composition analysis.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 were upregulated in the cycling immune cell subpopulation in degeneration samples.
source: We noticed some pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes upregulated in degeneration samples, for example, interleukin genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 upregulated in the cycling subpopulation (Figure 5A); chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 upregulated in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claim: Chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 were upregulated in macrophages/monocytes in degeneration samples.
source: We noticed some pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes upregulated in degeneration samples, for example, interleukin genes IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL15, and IL18 upregulated in the cycling subpopulation (Figure 5A); chemokine genes CXCL1, CCL3, and CXCL3 upregulated in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claim: Increased expressions of metallothionein genes MT1X and MT1G were observed in macrophages/monocytes in the degenerated group.
source: We also noticed increased expressions of metallothionein genes in the degenerated group, for example, MT1X and MT1G in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E in T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claim: Increased expressions of metallothionein genes MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E were observed in T cells in the degenerated group.
source: We also noticed increased expressions of metallothionein genes in the degenerated group, for example, MT1X and MT1G in macrophages/monocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), MT1X, MT2A, and MT1E in T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from differential gene expression analysis in immune cells.

claim: An arterial–capillary–venous gradient was identified in the meniscal endothelial cell population.
source: We identified an arterial–capillary–venous gradient in the meniscal endothelial cell population (Figure 5E–G) with other organs' endothelial markers (Schupp et al., 2021; Kalucka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from endothelial cell subtype analysis, using markers from other studies.

claim: The capillary–arterial endothelial cells highly express GJA5.
source: The capillary–arterial endothelial cells highly express GJA5; the capillary endothelial cells highly expressed PLVAP; and the capillary–venous endothelial cells highly expressed VWF.
evidence: This is an observation from endothelial cell marker expression analysis.

claim: The capillary endothelial cells highly expressed PLVAP.
source: The capillary–arterial endothelial cells highly express GJA5; the capillary endothelial cells highly expressed PLVAP; and the capillary–venous endothelial cells highly expressed VWF.
evidence: This is an observation from endothelial cell marker expression analysis.

claim: The capillary–venous endothelial cells highly expressed VWF.
source: The capillary–arterial endothelial cells highly express GJA5; the capillary endothelial cells highly expressed PLVAP; and the capillary–venous endothelial cells highly expressed VWF.
evidence: This is an observation from endothelial cell marker expression analysis.

claim: A tiny cluster of lymphatic endothelial cells was observed, which may come from the lymphatic vessels in the meniscus.
source: A tiny cluster of lymphatic endothelial cells was also observed, which may come from the lymphatic vessels in the meniscus.
evidence: This is an observation and inference from endothelial cell subtype analysis.

claim: In the normal group, CST3, ACKR1, RBP7, and IGFBP4 were upregulated in endothelial cells.
source: We compared the total endothelial cells between the normal/degenerated groups and reported a list of DEGs (Figure 5H). In the normal group, CST3, ACKR1, RBP7, and IGFBP4 were upregulated, while in the degenerated group, S100A4, DDIT4, CRIP1, and MGP were upregulated.
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis in endothelial cells.

claim: In the degenerated group, S100A4, DDIT4, CRIP1, and MGP were upregulated in endothelial cells.
source: We compared the total endothelial cells between the normal/degenerated groups and reported a list of DEGs (Figure 5H). In the normal group, CST3, ACKR1, RBP7, and IGFBP4 were upregulated, while in the degenerated group, S100A4, DDIT4, CRIP1, and MGP were upregulated.
evidence: This is a finding from differential gene expression analysis in endothelial cells.

claim: CST3 was reported to have inhibition effects on the proliferation, migration, tube formation, and permeability of endothelial cells.
source: CST3 is ranked first in the normal group DEGs, which was reported to have inhibition effects on the proliferation, migration, tube formation, and permeability of endothelial cells (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This references findings from Li et al., 2018 on CST3 function.

claim: ACKR1 encodes a chemokine decoy receptor inhibiting the effectiveness of other chemokines.
source: ACKR1 is also highly expressed in the normal group, which encodes a chemokine decoy receptor inhibiting the effectiveness of other chemokines (Rot, 2005).
evidence: This references findings from Rot, 2005 on ACKR1 function.

claim: CCI intensities generally increased in the degeneration group, especially for the endothelial cells and immune cells.
source: The results suggested that CCI intensities generally increased in the degeneration group, especially for the endothelial cells and immune cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In the degenerated meniscus, chemokine gene CXCL8 was upregulated by macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, DCs; and its receptor gene SDC2 was expressed in chondrocytes and the pericyte-like cells.
source: For example, in the degenerated meniscus, we observed that a chemokine gene CXCL8 was upregulated by macrophages/monocytes, neutrophils, DCs; and its receptor gene SDC2 was expressed in chondrocytes and the pericyte-like cells.
evidence: This is an observation from cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: Significant CALM1/2-INSR CCIs occurred in the degeneration in which angiogenesis happened – many cell types upregulated CALM1/2, and endothelial cells upregulated the insulin receptor gene INSR.
source: We also observed significant CALM1/2-INSR CCIs occurred in the degeneration in which angiogenesis happened – many cell types upregulated CALM1/2, and endothelial cells upregulated the insulin receptor gene INSR. This observation is consistent with a previous study showing insulin receptors' pro-angiogenesis functions. (Walker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an observation from cell-cell interaction analysis, consistent with a cited study.

claim: Multiple cell–cell crosstalks enhanced in the degeneration group are involved in immunoregulations and mediated by TNF superfamily interactions (TNF, TNFSF10 → VSIR, TNFRSF1A/B), TGF superfamily interactions (INHBA → ENG), and Class I HLA → APLP2 interactions.
source: We also identified multiple other cell–cell crosstalks enhanced in the degeneration group that are involved in immunoregulations. They are mediated by TNF superfamily interactions (TNF, TNFSF10 → VSIR, TNFRSF1A/B), and TGF superfamily interactions (INHBA → ENG), and Class I HLA → APLP2 interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: In normal meniscal tissues, the synthesis and disassembly of the matrix molecules were balanced in the orchestrated ECM metabolism.
source: In normal meniscal tissues, the synthesis and disassembly of the matrix molecules were balanced in the orchestrated ECM metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference about the homeostatic state based on the study's findings.

claim: The dominant Ch.1 population was essential to the balance maintenance because they expressed TIMP family molecules that inhibited the ECM decomposers (MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS).
source: We inferred that the dominant Ch.1 population was essential to the balance maintenance because they expressed TIMP family molecules that inhibited the ECM decomposers (MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS).
evidence: This is an inference based on Ch.1 marker expression and known TIMP function.

claim: The PCL population that adhered to the surface of endothelial cells maintained vasculature stability.
source: The PCL population that adhered to the surface of endothelial cells maintained vasculature stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on PCL localization and known pericyte function.

claim: The high-level expressions of atypical chemokine receptors like ACKR1 neutralized the chemokines and attenuated the angiogenesis.
source: The high-level expressions of atypical chemokine receptors like ACKR1 neutralized the chemokines and attenuated the angiogenesis (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on ACKR1 expression, supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of ECM decomposers (MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family molecules) from chondral subpopulations Ch.2 and Ch.3 might surpass the inhibition forces (TIMP) and decompose the ECM by breaking large PG molecules into fragments in degenerated meniscal tissues.
source: However, the balanced microenvironment was altered significantly in the degenerated meniscal tissues. The expression of ECM decomposers (MMP/ADAM/ADAMTS family molecules) from chondral subpopulations Ch.2 and Ch.3 might surpass the inhibition forces (TIMP) and decompose the ECM by breaking large PG molecules into fragments.
evidence: This is an inference about the degeneration mechanism based on gene expression patterns.

claim: Blood vessels can help to restore acute injuries to health but the proliferated blood vessels can build pathways for the immune cells so that they can infiltrate the meniscal matrix and cause inflammation.
source: We believe the blood vessels have two sides in the homeostasis of the meniscus. On the one hand, the blood vessels can help to restore acute injuries to health; on the other hand, the proliferated blood vessels can build pathways for the immune cells so that they can infiltrate the meniscal matrix and cause inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference about the dual role of blood vessels based on the study's observations.

claim: The detachment and decrease of the pericyte may lead to pathological states.
source: While the pericyte stabilizes the blood vessel in health, the detachment and decrease of the pericyte may lead to pathological states (Figueiredo et al., 2020; Armulik et al., 2011; Diéguez-Hurtado et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies on pericyte function.

claim: Changing the chondrocyte subtype ratios and limiting blood vessel proliferation may delay or reverse the meniscus degeneration.
source: Changing the chondrocyte subtype ratios and limiting blood vessel proliferation may delay or reverse the meniscus degeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication based on the study's findings.

claim: Females make up the majority of the study's donors.
source: Another limitation of this study is that females make up the majority of our donors (Supplementary file 1), since OA is more common in middle-aged and older females.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding the study design.

claim: The cellular profiles observed in this study may better represent the female population.
source: The cellular profiles observed in this study may better represent the female population.
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of the findings based on the donor demographics.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms observed in this study on meniscal degeneration, such as angiogenesis and inflammation, could also apply to intervertebral discs and articular cartilage degeneration.
source: We speculated that the cellular and molecular mechanisms observed in this study on meniscal degeneration, such as angiogenesis and inflammation, could also apply to intervertebral discs and articular cartilage degeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings to other cartilage tissues.
